knowledge.question: How should I test a new product without risking too much?
knowledge.answer: Buy from local suppliers where you can test with smaller quantities, even at a slightly higher unit cost. Levi told one supplier he'd put $5,000 into a minimum order: with his experience, the worst case is he breaks even, and since the supplier is down the road he gets it the next day instead of waiting a month from China. Don't put too much money into one product in case it flops, and keep testing different products.

knowledge.question: How do I find better suppliers for Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Go to trade shows and network. Levi says you'd never find some suppliers otherwise, even ones two or three blocks away, because they don't focus on social media; they've been around for years selling to brick-and-mortar stores like Ollie's, Dollar Tree and Family Dollar. He went to a Las Vegas trade show to widen his catalog, which already has over a thousand SKUs.

knowledge.question: Should I pay suppliers with a credit card?
knowledge.answer: Levi recommends looking at a business card like a Chase card that gives about 2.2% cash back on spending under $5K, especially if the supplier already charges a processing fee for cards. A credit card also protects you: one of his students paid a pallet seller with American Express, got scammed, and got refunded.

knowledge.question: How do I avoid getting scammed buying pallets?
knowledge.answer: Levi warns that pallet scams are common on Facebook and often target new sellers. A typical scam: they say they'll ship you the pallet, charge a $500 insurance fee, then claim it was lost and ask for more; they may even sell under popular people's names. Buy locally where you can go to the seller's warehouse, meet them, and take the pallet home that day. Paying with a card like American Express can get you refunded.

knowledge.question: What are the best days to go live on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi's best days are Sundays and Mondays, and Chase's are Saturdays and Sundays. Holidays can be huge: Chase's biggest day was Christmas, about $8,700 in 4-5 hours, because fewer sellers stream and bored buyers are on the app; Levi found Thanksgiving Thursday very good too. Levi says Whatnot's 0% fee day was actually bad, with too many sellers and buyers swiping between shows looking for deals. He also finds Fridays hard.

knowledge.question: Can I sell on Whatnot while working full-time or in school?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Levi says 2-3 hours of live a day can take you a long way; one follower working full-time did $14,000 in their first seven streams with $10,000 profit. Chase is a full-time college student who runs his business from home with his mom streaming in the mornings and his brother packing after school.

knowledge.question: When should I delegate streaming to other people?
knowledge.answer: Levi points out most people want to do everything themselves. Once you reach a certain level, delegating streaming to other streamers gives you more time to source inventory and see what's going wrong or right in the business so you can capitalize on it.

knowledge.question: Where can I get free shipping boxes for Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: USPS Priority Mail and flat rate boxes are free; order them on usps.com. Levi still thinks buying your own boxes is worth it when buyers usually buy more than six items, since six items could be around $16 and a box is about a dollar. He also runs unlimited bundles and will split heavy orders into multiple shipments, paying $5 here or there out of pocket, because buyers end up buying more.

knowledge.question: How do I decide which products to reorder?
knowledge.answer: Levi asks Chase, who reorders items making over $5 profit, ideally $5-10, that sell through quickly or that buyers request. Items that profit well but move slowly get restocked less or not at all. They also favor small items that fit in bubble mailers and don't need bubble wrap, because they're cheap and fast to ship.

knowledge.question: Is Whatnot or TikTok better for live sellers?
knowledge.answer: Levi thinks Whatnot may be better in certain ways. TikTok is great for businesses trying to scale and hire quickly because you can open multiple accounts, which is what he did. But on Whatnot you sell about twice as fast, and bids can be a bit lower or sometimes even higher than on TikTok. He plans to run consistent 16-24 hour streams on Whatnot for two weeks to compare the full math, and his hypothesis is that Whatnot comes out ahead.

knowledge.question: How do cancellations and shipping compare between TikTok and Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi sees much higher cancellation rates on TikTok: around 30 out of every 600 units get cancelled or fail payment because buyers don't know how to fix their payment. On about $55,000 a month in GMV, that adds up to around $8,000 in refunds. On Whatnot he has lost only about $5,000 over $1.5 million in sales, not even close to 1%. Whatnot also ships about 50% faster for his team because buyers purchase big bundles and one-item orders are rare, while TikTok has lots of one-unit orders.

knowledge.question: When do I get paid for my sales on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: As a beginner, you don't get paid until about 4 hours after the package is delivered. Levi's account gets paid out as soon as labels are printed, but that's not where beginners start. That's why he recommends beginners use priority mail only: the faster it's delivered, the faster you get your money and can reinvest.

knowledge.question: What is a video receipt and how do I use it?
knowledge.answer: In Shipments, each order has a video receipt showing the moment the buyer won the item, available going back about 90 days. Pull it up when a customer complains to see exactly what they bought. Receipts are usually slightly off, often showing the next item, and get less accurate the longer the show runs. Levi likes using it on the phone, where you can search any lot number by date and skip forward or back 10 seconds. Showing the lot number on camera when you can builds buyer confidence.

knowledge.question: Can I switch a label to a large flat rate box after packing?
knowledge.answer: Yes, and it's free if your shipping is priority mail. If a bundle ends up heavier than 5 lb, go to edit shipping information, toggle on the large flat rate box, update the label and reprint it. It doesn't count as a weekly label adjustment because a large flat rate box (12x12x8, up to 70 lb) costs less than a priority mail large shipping box, so it's a downgrade. Never put a large flat rate label on a box that doesn't say flat rate on it.

knowledge.question: How do label adjustments and the weekly allowance work?
knowledge.answer: Changing a label within the price the buyer already paid is $0; for example, 60 oz costs the same as 80 oz, and switching to large flat rate is free. It only costs you if you go over 80 oz; Levi showed going to 160 oz costs about $3. You get five free label adjustments per week, and his team rarely uses them.

knowledge.question: What do I do if a bundle doesn't fit in one box?
knowledge.answer: Use unbundle shipment in Shipments, choose the item(s) to take out, and click unbundle selected items. It creates a separate shipment with its own weight. Levi's trick: each of the two boxes can be set up to 80 oz and it still only counts as one shipping allowance, because all you did was unbundle.

knowledge.question: What is a USPS scan sheet and why should I use one?
knowledge.answer: A scan sheet lets USPS scan one sheet at pickup and mark every package on it as accepted, like 250 at once, instead of scanning each box. Generate it in Shipments after printing labels (refresh the page if the option doesn't show). Levi says everyone, beginner or advanced, should use them, especially in Q4, because USPS can take days to check in packages and Whatnot will flag you as late. His advice: don't drop off without a scan sheet.

knowledge.question: What if I forgot to use a scan sheet and packages show as not dropped off?
knowledge.answer: Scan it in anyway, even if it's late. Levi tells his shippers he'd rather the system flag orders as late than show them as never dropped off. If a customer says they didn't receive an order and it never checked in, Whatnot refunds them and you take a ding. Late check-ins only lowered his account health a bit (99.35% with 300 late scans in 90 days).

knowledge.question: How should I set up small, medium and large shipping profiles?
knowledge.answer: Different shipping profiles never mix in a bundle. Levi's small profile can be 15 oz per item with a max of 5, or 75 oz for the first item and 1 oz for each item after, so the bundle averages about 80 oz and stays in the $9.21 1-5 lb priority mail range. Medium is about 79 to 80 oz with a max of two items. Large is 80 oz with a max of one item and nothing added. He doesn't like Whatnot's default AI smart bundling because it doesn't set a max.

knowledge.question: How does a fill-a-box listing work?
knowledge.answer: Create a shipping profile, for example called fill a box, at 80 oz (5 lb) with a max of one item, and use it on a listing that says fill a box. On camera you take a flat rate box and fill it up, and it doesn't matter how much it weighs. At the end, in Shipments, you change that 5 lb priority mail label to a large flat rate box label for free. Other selling methods he mentions are two-item bundles, buyer's choice and mystery picks.

knowledge.question: What shipping settings should I choose in the Whatnot app?
knowledge.answer: In the phone app, go to Seller Hub, then shipping settings (you can't do this on the laptop). Levi recommends choosing priority mail for 1-5 lb and priority mail for over 5 lb. If you ever need to downgrade later, it's cheaper.

knowledge.question: Why are buyers saying they lost their free shipping during my show?
knowledge.answer: Don't edit your shipping profiles or your listings' shipping profiles while you're live, because it resets everybody's bundle. Levi did it once and got lots of comments asking where free shipping went, and his brother had the same issue. The app also glitches on its own about once a day. The fix is for the buyer to exit the show or app and come back in; if they already bid while it showed a shipping charge, they have to contact Whatnot to get it fixed.

knowledge.question: Should I print labels as I go or all at once?
knowledge.answer: End the show and print all the labels at once before you start shipping. Levi's team prints around 250 labels at a time. You end up with a stack and always know how many orders are left. If you keep looking at the screen, you'll lose track of where you started, where to end, and which orders you've done.

knowledge.question: How should I lay out a warehouse for Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi says open space is your best friend: don't put pallet racks in the middle of the floor. He moved his racks against the wall and it made the whole operation far more efficient, leaving a large open area just for shipping. His shipping area runs two packers when needed and two pickers working on the boxes.

knowledge.question: Should I sell straight from pallets or put inventory on shelves?
knowledge.answer: Levi moved everything off pallets and onto racks. A 6-foot pallet hides what's at the bottom, and digging through it during a show was inefficient. On shelves you can see every product, which lets you sell faster and know exactly what's left; for example, seeing four dozen keychains left tells you to keep running them back to back. The only pallets left in his warehouse are outgoing shipments.

knowledge.question: What racks should I buy for my streaming and shipping area?
knowledge.answer: Levi bought 20 more 86-inch, five-tier racks on Temu for about $2,000; the extra tier helps, but the wheels aren't great, so he doesn't load them too heavy. He also got 20 racks on Facebook Marketplace for about $1,200-1,300, roughly $80 each, which were more durable and had better wheels. His advice is to invest in racks with wheels because it makes the operation much smoother.

knowledge.question: Does my stream background matter once I have regular buyers?
knowledge.answer: Levi says that for an established seller, the background matters less. His account, 12 months in, gets around 100 repeat buyers every day who know and trust them, so they don't care much about the background. He admits a nicer background might attract new customers.

knowledge.question: What should I do when my main product runs out of supply?
knowledge.answer: Don't stop the business and don't let people go; go hunting for a solution. Levi used to get a truckload of backpacks a week (they sold around 20,000 in March), then got only one truckload in four weeks. Because his main account has buyers who trust what they sell, he switched to keychains sourced at 40 cents each to keep multiple streams running.

knowledge.question: How do I make good profit on cheap items like keychains?
knowledge.answer: Bundle them, because people buy more when you bundle. Levi pays 40 cents per keychain and sells them around $4-5 each; he's gotten four for $26, which cost him $1.60. A five-pack costs him $2.50, and even at a $15 average sale he makes $11-12 per bundle. At about $10 profit per bundle and 100 bundles a day, that's $1,000 a day; he conservatively expects $20,000 a month in profit from keychains, and they're very easy to ship.

knowledge.question: Can I negotiate prices with my suppliers?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Levi sources keychains at 40 cents each and still plans to negotiate the rates down to get them even cheaper. Lowering your buy cost on items you sell in volume increases your profit on every bundle.

knowledge.question: Why switch from Amazon to Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi says Whatnot gives you the flexibility to sell pretty much whatever you want, which Amazon no longer does. Big Amazon sellers 15–20 years ago started with liquidation and closeouts, but now you have to get ungated, and those restrictions slow your growth and profit. Amazon also keeps adding fees because, as a public company, it cares about shareholders, while Whatnot is private and growing.

knowledge.question: Do I need a big social media following to succeed on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: No. Levi calls that a misconception: he had 1,800 Instagram followers before Whatnot, downloaded the app at 5 a.m., scheduled his live for 1 p.m., and did $3,000 in sales knowing nothing. Buyers find you on Whatnot itself, which brings new buyers to the app every day, so it's very difficult not to sell something.

knowledge.question: What's the most important tip for a new reseller?
knowledge.answer: Stay consistent, because this does not happen overnight. Levi started with $500 in 2020 and went through multiple businesses, and he says Whatnot is the number one platform right now for beginner resellers.

knowledge.question: Where can I find inventory to sell on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi's three main methods are: Facebook Marketplace and Facebook liquidation groups, which have a lot of gold; trade shows like the Las Vegas ASD show, the closeout show in Las Vegas, and WHSL, a trade show made specifically for liquidation; and, once you scale, buying from China. He doesn't think China is necessary because there's a ton of supply in the US. Liquidation goes deeper than you think, with pallets as low as $100 to $150 and Target loads as cheap as $1 per piece if you look.

knowledge.question: How do I avoid getting scammed when buying pallets?
knowledge.answer: Buy in person, FaceTime, or call the seller, and if you really can't get in contact with them, don't buy. A common scam is the seller saying they need you to pay insurance on the load, then coming up with another reason to collect more money. One of Levi's students got scammed but paid with an American Express card and got refunded easily. Start local so you can see and touch the product and avoid freight charges.

knowledge.question: What kind of inventory should a beginner buy?
knowledge.answer: Levi recommends everyone start with a local liquidation pallet because it's a mix of inventory at a very low cost. On the East Coast, Target loads do very well; you can buy them at about 5% to 25% of retail depending on the product. Go in person, touch the product, make sure it's real, and keep your cost per unit low. On the West Coast near the ports, you can find cheap wholesale electronics and clothing.

knowledge.question: Is it better to have lots of one product or lots of different products?
knowledge.answer: Variety. Levi would rather have a thousand different products than a thousand of one product. People on Whatnot aren't buying things they need; they're buying things they want on a random day and trying to fill their boxes. If you only have 20 different products and 80 viewers, the chances they fill their bundles drop, so you need a mix that gets people competing with each other.

knowledge.question: How do I know my real cost per unit on a pallet?
knowledge.answer: Count everything and divide what you paid by the number of units. Levi's friend in Arizona was told a pallet of electronics would be about $2.40 a unit, but after counting it came to $2.15, about 10% cheaper. Your actual cost can be lower than what the supplier tells you.

knowledge.question: When should I buy a large quantity of a single product?
knowledge.answer: Only after you've tested it. Levi test-bought a thousand different products to learn what people pay in an auction environment, and now knows items like scooters, wallets and certain brands well enough that buyers pay over 50% of retail. One Altec speaker came in a mixed load, sold well, and he's since sold at least 8,000 of them; he'd buy a whole truckload now. Don't try to copy someone else's products exactly, because they're getting different rates, pricing and freight than you.

knowledge.question: Should I do $1 starts or higher starting prices?
knowledge.answer: You don't have to do $1 starts. Many of Levi's students run $5 starts and do very well, which helps guarantee profit, especially in the beginning. Levi himself moves a lot of volume at low starts so he can lock in contracts at even cheaper rates and then also wholesale inventory.

knowledge.question: How do I get buyers to fill up their shipping boxes?
knowledge.answer: Match your bundle to the box you're paying for. Levi uses 18x12x8 boxes that fit 10 items, so he runs a 10-item bundle, and at least 40 people fill their box every day. A wide mix of products is what makes people keep adding items. Also know your buyers: his cater to moms, people who donate, resellers and exporters, so his product holds value for all of them.

knowledge.question: Can I run a Whatnot business without being where my inventory and shipping team are?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Levi describes a seller who has been on Whatnot for nearly three years and built his business so he can go live from anywhere, as long as he has a display of the product in stock. His stock and fulfillment team are in Washington DC and ship everything sold the night before, so he can take a suitcase of displays on a trip and stream from a hotel room. Another seller in California has his employees stream from home while he supplies the product and handles fulfillment.

knowledge.question: What kind of profit margins can I expect on Whatnot compared to Amazon FBA?
knowledge.answer: Levi says on Amazon FBA you are dealing with roughly 10-15% margins, while on Whatnot you are dealing with 40%-plus margins, and it can go as high as 80%. The tradeoff is that Whatnot requires more people; it is the first business where he has had more than five employees.

knowledge.question: What is the hardest part of scaling a Whatnot business?
knowledge.answer: Levi says one of the biggest struggles is finding reliable employees, and hiring is very tough, especially for management roles. That is why he likes the idea of a model where a seller only focuses on selling and being a good salesperson, while someone else handles fulfillment and customer service.

knowledge.question: Do buyers care that my streamers are employees and not the owner?
knowledge.answer: Not in a bad way. Levi says his buyers know his streamers are not the owner, but they trust any account he owns or anyone he recommends, so they buy from them too. Trust carries across the accounts run by him, his dad, his brother and his friends, so everyone's business feeds off each other.

knowledge.question: Is it too late to start selling on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi says no. In electronics, the category he sells in most, there are only about 80 sellers a day and around 8,000-9,000 viewers max, and the viewership has doubled since September while the number of sellers has not. With 300 million people in the US and many still not knowing what Whatnot is, he says if you are on the app now, you are already early.

knowledge.question: Can I change the shipping weight for each item number on Whatnot to get more accurate postage?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Levi explains that as long as you use the Whatnot shipping profile rather than your own custom shipping profile, you can set a different weight for each numbered listing (for example, number 1 at 7 oz and number 2 at 15 oz), and Whatnot will still bundle them automatically. Using the actual weight instead of an average means buyers do not overpay on postage. You just account for roughly one extra pound for the box or poly mailer at the end.

knowledge.question: Do I have to sell liquidation to have a Whatnot business?
knowledge.answer: No. Levi says liquidation and closeouts are what he focuses on (buying at about 10% of retail or under), but you can also buy from China in bulk, keep enough stock, and grow your own business from that.

knowledge.question: What's the best category to start selling on Whatnot as a beginner?
knowledge.answer: Levi always recommends students start with health and beauty. There are hundreds of millions of liquidation units sitting in warehouses that owners don't know how to move, the products are small and light, and the risk of losing money is low. Just make sure items are not expired and not used.

knowledge.question: How cheap can I buy health and beauty liquidation inventory?
knowledge.answer: Levi bought pallets of health and beauty products for $600 each, with roughly 1,500 to 1,800 units per pallet, putting the buy cost under 50 cents per unit. He sold bobby pins from those pallets at four for $5, while the supplier had been throwing out pallets of the same stuff. He says he pays an average max of $1.50 per item for health and beauty.

knowledge.question: Why do buyers stay in health and beauty shows so long?
knowledge.answer: Levi says people buy on Whatnot for great deals and shipping. Once they buy one item, committed buyers are locked into your show for at least an hour filling their bundle. Health and beauty rarely goes over $10 per item, so on a 10-item bundle they'd pay at most about $100 and are happy paying $9.21 shipping for all of it.

knowledge.question: How do I set up 'buy two, get the next eight free' shipping on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Go to shipping profiles, create a custom shipping profile, set a maximum bundle of 10 and make it 8 ounces per item. Once buyers purchase two items, they'll see free shipping at the bottom of the screen for the next eight items, and you have to clarify this to all your buyers. Two items at 8 oz each equal one pound, which puts the order into Priority Mail at $9.21, and the 10-item cap means it never goes over five pounds.

knowledge.question: Why cap bundles at 10 items instead of offering unlimited bundles?
knowledge.answer: Levi caps at 10 because on average 10 items fit perfectly in a flat rate box, and it gives shippers a clear standard at volume (his team ships 1,200 to 1,600 beauty units a day). He doesn't recommend unlimited bundles: the box dimension is 12x12x12, so 50 items won't fit, you have to split the shipment, you may be charged for it, and you only get about five label changes per week at no cost.

knowledge.question: How do I use flat rate labels to save on shipping?
knowledge.answer: At the end of the show, select all the Priority Mail labels and convert them to flat rate labels. Even if a buyer's bundle is five pounds, the Priority Mail cost is $9.21 and a flat rate label up to 70 pounds is also $9.21. Just make sure you actually put those orders in a flat rate box when you use a flat rate label.

knowledge.question: How do my shippers know what box to use?
knowledge.answer: Levi makes it simple: a Priority Mail label means two items or more, so shippers always use a large flat rate box or large Priority Mail box for 2 to 10 items, since buyers paid for up to a 12x12x12 dimension. A ground label means it's a one-item order, which rarely happens in health and beauty because people won't pay $3–$6 for an item plus $4–$6 shipping.

knowledge.question: How much do I need to invest to start in health and beauty?
knowledge.answer: Levi says at about $1 to $1.50 per unit, an investment of $500 to $1,000 gets you roughly 500 to 1,000 units. It's a low-cost way to build your account while still making a profit.

knowledge.question: What kind of profit can I expect from health and beauty on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi's example: buy at $1, sell at $5, and Whatnot fees on health and beauty are roughly 20%, leaving about $4, which is $3 profit on a $1 investment, or 300% return. He says high-ticket categories like electronics, tools and shoes usually aren't seeing 100–300% returns. Profit is very predictable because there are no returns or cancellations.

knowledge.question: What fees does Whatnot charge on beauty sales?
knowledge.answer: Levi lists the category fee (he mentions 5%/8% for beauty), the 2.9% processing fee, and 30 cents per transaction. He says there are no extra fees, so it's very easy to predict your profit.

knowledge.question: Is it only makeup I can sell in health and beauty?
knowledge.answer: No. Levi says it doesn't have to be liquid makeup; you can also sell brushes and bobby pins. Brushes are actually top sellers, and he'd buy a thousand brushes at a dollar a piece.

knowledge.question: How can I set up a bonus system to motivate my live stream hosts?
knowledge.answer: Levi pays his streamers $18 an hour and layers volume bonuses on top. In one week's promotion, a streamer who sold 1,000 items in a shift got an extra $100, and doing that 5 days in a row earned an extra $200 on top, for up to $700 in bonuses beyond base pay. He says a lot of streamers hit it, and he decides week to week whether to run it again depending on how it goes.

knowledge.question: Does having different hosts on my Whatnot account help the business?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Levi says many of his top streamer Kristen's buyers don't show up to his shows because they just don't vibe with him, and that's fine. From a business perspective, it brings in new and returning customers for that streamer that you wouldn't get if you were selling alone.

knowledge.question: Does the category a host sells change who watches and bids?
knowledge.answer: Yes. On a new account, Levi's female host sold a lot of unisex products and attracted more men, who gave her higher bids and very good pricing. When she switched to bedding, the male customers left and the bidding changed. He notes that putting a female host on beauty products might actually get lower viewership.

knowledge.question: I only have 10-20 viewers. Is anyone actually watching?
knowledge.answer: Yes, more than you think. Levi says a beginner fluctuating between 10 and 20 viewers usually has at least 100 to 200 people watching for more than 30 seconds each hour, and you can see this in your live stream analytics. When his show peaked at 300 viewers, around 6,000 people had watched over the 4-6 hour show. Whatnot is sending you traffic; your job is to convert those viewers into buyers.

knowledge.question: How do I find out who is new in my show?
knowledge.answer: Whatnot shows who joins your live only while you're under 60 viewers. After that, do a welcome-in every 5 to 10 minutes: 'If you're new here, comment me.' Levi often gets 30 people out of 150 saying they're new, because the algorithm is always sending new people. Once you know who's new, treat them as new customers and offer them something special.

knowledge.question: What do new buyers not understand that I need to explain?
knowledge.answer: They don't know about your free shipping, and they don't know the show notes are at the top left unless you tell them to click. When people say they're new, explain shipping right away: they only pay shipping on the first item, and the next however many are free, based on your max bundle. Levi says new sellers forget that the app is new to lots of buyers every day too.

knowledge.question: How do I make an ordinary item sound worth buying?
knowledge.answer: Gas it up and prove it. Levi's example was $35-40 wireless headphones you could get in any Target truckload: he called out up to 40 hours of playback, that they're wireless and wired, that the aux cord and charging cable are included, and the 33-foot range. Tell them why they should buy it. Even standard features sell when you present them with energy.

knowledge.question: Should I tell my viewers the prices are too low?
knowledge.answer: No. Levi's streamers started getting a little aggressive in the first months, saying things like 'come on, the prices are too low,' and he says never do that. Make people feel welcome, ask your buyers for feedback (is shipping fast enough, do you like the items), and test new items based on what they want.

knowledge.question: Should I do $1 starts or higher fixed starts like $49?
knowledge.answer: Either can work. With $1 starts, expect to lose money on the first 40 to 50 items while you convert viewers into buyers. Levi knows sellers who do $39 to $69 starts, or $49 starts on shoes and apparel that retail for $80 to $100 and cost them $15 to $25, and they do well. But those shows can go 30 minutes without a sale, and most people don't have the patience for that.

knowledge.question: Why do fast, cheap auctions get more traffic from Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Whatnot makes money when you make money, so it sends more traffic to sellers making more money per second. Levi's math: a $5 sale every 5 seconds is 12 sales a minute, or $60 a minute, compared to a $49 sale every 15 to 30 minutes. Hit the algorithm by making sales. He says you have to lose to win sometimes, give deals, and make people come back.

knowledge.question: Should I judge my profit item by item?
knowledge.answer: No, look at it per load. Levi doesn't care if one item sells at a loss because the next might sell for $10. If you pay $5,000 for 2,500 units, your cost is $2 a unit, and that's what you measure against. Remember the fees too; he mentions about 5% per transaction plus 2.9% and 30 cents processing. When several buyers compete to fill their bundles, prices go up and you're profitable on most items day to day.
